source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese Riddles Reveal Fundamental Limits of Machine Insight and Self-Evaluation in Reasoning AI (NazoNazo)
finding: Children's riddles that need a representation shift are very hard for most models. Reasoning models do better than non-reasoning ones, but still far below humans. Only GPT-5 reached the human range.
numbers: 201 riddles; human reference n=126 on a 120-item subset, mean 52.9% (95% CI 46.6-59.2). 38 LLMs, zero-shot, no retrieval: non-reasoning 7.6%, reasoning 17.6% on the subset. Full 201 items: 9.42% vs 19.25%, odds ratio 2.29 (95% CI 1.99-2.64). Parameter count did not predict accuracy; release date did.
quote: models generate a correct intermediate candidate but fail to endorse it as their final answer
limits: Observational comparison. GPT-5 inside the human CI is not proof of equivalence. Public riddles, some contamination risk. Japanese wordplay, so partly a language-form test.
agent_relevance: Insight-type items are a real weak spot even for reasoning models. Score them by checking, not by the model's own sense of being done.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) NazoNazo, verification-failure analysis
finding: In thought logs the model often writes the right answer and then walks away from it. This is a failure to endorse a correct candidate, not a failure to generate it.
numbers: Verification failures = share of wrong answers where a gold answer appears in the thought log: Gemini 2.5 Flash Preview 5.23%, DeepSeek-R1-0528 30.57%, Claude Opus 4 25.00%, Grok 4 39.34% (4 models with usable logs).
quote: verification failures account for between 5% and 39% of a model's incorrect answers
limits: Detected by literal string match in the log, so it can over-count (an answer mentioned and rejected for good reason). Only 4 models. Logs may be unfaithful.
agent_relevance: Strong case for harvesting every candidate from the trace (S4) and testing each with code, rather than trusting the final line. Links to the verification-design and stopping subfields.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) NazoNazo, thought-log language and false insight
finding: The language the model reasons in (English vs Japanese) did not help in a consistent way. Some traces show a confident wrong reinterpretation, which the authors compare to false insight in humans.
numbers: Grok 4: Japanese logs 29.5% (33/112) vs English logs 48.8% (40/82), Fisher p=0.0071. Claude Opus 4: 36.7% vs 28.7%, p=0.356. Gemini 2.5 Flash: 0% (0/12) vs 11.7% (22/188), p=0.369.
limits: Language choice is not randomised (model picks it), so it is confounded with item difficulty. Only one of four models is significant.
agent_relevance: A wrong confident re-framing is a second failure mode next to non-endorsement. A reframe operator needs a check that can reject a bad frame.

source: d'Aliberti and Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models
finding: Spontaneous mid-reasoning shifts (the 'aha' cue) are rare and usually go with lower accuracy, not higher. They do not grow with RL training. Cryptic crosswords were used as the representational-change domain.
numbers: GRPO fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-1.5B (1000 steps), Qwen2.5-7B and Llama3.1-8B (500 steps), domains: cryptic crosswords, MATH-500, RHour. Pooled shift rate 6.31%. Accuracy without vs with shift (pooled) 0.290 vs 0.066. Math 1.5B: 0.327 vs 0.144 (2.65% of traces). Crosswords 1.5B: 0.096 vs 0.201 (1.22% of traces, shifted traces better here). Qwen-7B math 0.661 vs 0.282. DeepSeek-R1 shift rate 0.40-0.60%, GPT-4o 2.20-3.00%. Traces: about 320,000 math, 83,200 crossword, 320,000 RHour per 1.5B run.
quote: reasoning shifts are rare, do not become more frequent with training, and seldom improve accuracy
limits: Shifts detected by GPT-4o judge plus cue prefilter. Small models mostly. Crossword base accuracy is only 7.7-10%, so crossword estimates are noisy. Selection effect: a model that is already failing is the one that pivots.
agent_relevance: Do not count on the model to re-represent by itself mid-trace. Supports G1: trigger the reframe from outside, on a signal.

source: d'Aliberti and Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight, forced reconsideration
finding: Adding an external reconsideration cue to a second pass raises accuracy a lot on math and only a little on crosswords. The gain is larger when the first pass had high token entropy.
numbers: Cue example: 'Wait, something is not right, we need to reconsider. Let's think this through step by step.' Paired Pass 1 vs Pass 2: Math 32.21% to 40.62% (wins 50,574 vs losses 23,500). Crosswords 9.70% to 10.15% (wins 5,380 vs losses 5,004). RHour near zero (100 vs 58 wins). Gates: top 20% entropy vs bottom 80%.
limits: Pass 2 is also a second sample, so part of the gain may be plain resampling. The paper has an appendix on this but the main contrast is not against a neutral resample. Only small models. Crossword (representation-change) gain is tiny.
agent_relevance: A cheap, signal-gated reconsider pass works for math but barely for representation-hard items. A generic 'think again' is not a re-representation operator; test O6 against a neutral resample at equal tokens (G7).

source: Kang et al. (2025) First Try Matters: Revisiting the Role of Reflection in Reasoning Models
finding: After a model writes its first candidate answer, the later 'reflection' almost never changes it. Reflection is mostly confirmation.
numbers: 8 reasoning models (7B to 685B), 5 math sets, 3,427 rollouts per model. Over 90% of reflections are confirmatory (right to right, wrong to wrong same). Wrong-to-right changes mostly under 2%. Extractor judged correct on 94% of 426 candidates (100 rollouts, human check). Truncating reflection after a candidate cuts reasoning tokens 24.5% with a 2.9% accuracy drop.
quote: reflections are largely confirmatory and rarely corrective
limits: Math only, where re-representation is rarely needed. LLM-based extractor. SFT on more reflections helped first-answer correctness, not self-correction.
agent_relevance: Same message as c04 from a second angle: in-trace reflection is not a re-representation engine. Spend tokens on fresh restatements, not on longer reflection.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) BRAINTEASER: Lateral Thinking Puzzles for Large Language Models
finding: Models fall far behind humans on puzzles that need default commonsense to be dropped. They also fail when the same puzzle is reworded or moved to a new context, which points to memory and surface association, not a change of representation.
numbers: 1,100 puzzles (sentence and word). Human (3 experts, 102 items) about 92%. Random 25%. Best model ChatGPT 53% and 63% on the two subtasks. ChatGPT and RoBERTa-L fail 45% and 61% of originals that they solve in context-reconstructed form. Few-shot demos (2, 4, 6, 8): no clear effect on sentence puzzles. Commonsense-knowledge-adapted models did worse on sentence puzzles.
quote: commonsense knowledge has a salient negative impact on the model's performance on sentence puzzles
limits: Multiple choice, so guessing and elimination help. 2023 models. Table layout in the PDF text was garbled, so subtask-level numbers other than the quoted summary were not used.
agent_relevance: Group-consistency across rewordings (original + semantic + context variants) is a code-checkable test that a solution came from structure, not recall. Candidate for G3 on riddle-like problems.

source: Jiang, Ilievski, Ma (2024) SemEval-2024 Task 9: BRAINTEASER
finding: Many systems hit near ceiling on the headline score but almost all lose accuracy when the puzzle is reworded or moved to a new context. Fine-tuning learns shortcuts; prompting struggles to find the general lateral pattern.
numbers: 483 submissions from 182 participants. Baselines: human 0.920, ChatGPT 0.627. Best systems reach 100% on instance accuracy. More than 80% of leaderboard systems lose accuracy on original+semantic: 0.025-0.175 (sentence), 0.031-0.281 (word); on original+semantic+context: 0.025-0.275 and 0.031-0.344. Zero-shot or few-shot prompting best on word puzzles; fine-tuned small models best on sentence puzzles. Humor/riddle data helped.
limits: Scored on a 20% subset of the benchmark; authors expect lateral patterns to recur between train and test, which favours fine-tuning.
agent_relevance: Headline scores on insight-style sets overstate ability. Use perturbed variants to test whether a reframe was real.

source: Panagiotopoulos et al. (2024) RISCORE: Enhancing In-Context Riddle Solving through Context-Reconstructed Example Augmentation
finding: Giving the model examples that share the same reasoning pattern but sit in a new context beats picking examples by surface similarity. Chain-of-thought few-shot did worse than plain few-shot on BrainTeaser.
numbers: BrainTeaser, hand-made reconstructions: Llama3-70B 2+2 shot RISCORE 0.833 vs 4-shot similarity-selected 0.792 (the 2-shot similarity baseline was 0.825). Mistral-7B 0.567 vs 0.458. Automated version: Llama3-70B 8-shot 0.808 vs 0.783; Qwen2-7B about +2.5%; Mistral-7B up to +10% from 0.458. RiddleSense: Llama3-8B 0.708 vs 0.681; Mistral-8x7B 0.700 vs 0.675.
limits: Small models and small test sets. Hand-curated version is an upper bound. Gains are 2-10 points. Example choice may matter because of leakage of patterns.
agent_relevance: Reframing by pattern, not by topic, is the useful part. A re-representation step could retrieve prior solved cases by structure.

source: Huang et al. (2024) LatEval: An Interactive LLMs Evaluation Benchmark with Incomplete Information from Lateral Thinking Puzzles
finding: In an interactive yes/no puzzle game, models ask many questions but few that move toward the hidden story. They can integrate clues when given them, but not find them.
numbers: GPT-4 as host, English: answer consistency (AC) GPT-4 34.2, GPT-3.5 17.1, Claude 14.5; question relevance (QR) 58.4, 53.3, 49.6. With GPT-3.5 host, GPT-4 AC 27.5. With more clues given, deduction improves for GPT-4/GPT-3.5. Host accuracy over 90% (GPT-4) and over 80% (GPT-3.5).
quote: most models lack the ability to extract essential information from questioning
limits: Scores depend on a GPT-4 judge/host; AC is a similarity-style score, not exact solution rate. Chain-of-thought not tested.
agent_relevance: Question-asking to probe the hidden structure is a weak skill. Links to the probing and measurement-selection subfield.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Weak-eval-Strong: Evaluating and Eliciting Lateral Thinking of LLMs with Situation Puzzles (SPLAT)
finding: Situation puzzles give a graded benchmark where accuracy falls steeply with difficulty. Putting the question-and-answer transcript of one solved puzzle into the prompt improved other lateral benchmarks.
numbers: 975 puzzles, 3 levels. Judge agreement with humans above 80% (WizardLM-2 as judge). GPT-4 accuracy easy 70.96, medium 36.88, hard 17.27, average 41.70; Llama3-70B average 34.50; Llama3-8B 17.05. Auxiliary prompt from 1 puzzle (first 5 turns): RiddleSense Llama3-8B 70.51 to 72.18, 70B 83.34 to 85.21, GPT-4 88.83 to 89.23. BrainTeaser word puzzle: Llama3-8B 46.20 to 58.07, 70B 71.20 to 79.54, GPT-4 64.39 to 69.69; sentence: GPT-4 88.95 to 91.88.
limits: The prompt is a worked transcript from the same family, so part of the gain is format/example effect. m=1 puzzle only. Gains on RiddleSense for GPT-4 are 0.4 points.
agent_relevance: A small worked example of hypothesis-testing questions can lift lateral-style tasks, especially word puzzles. Cheap to try, but measure at equal tokens (G7).

source: Todd et al. (2024) Missed Connections: Lateral Thinking Puzzles for Large Language Models
finding: Grouping 16 words into 4 themes needs seeing words under uncommon readings while ignoring red herrings. Chain-of-thought helps GPT-4 on the standard game but not when the puzzle is made harder.
numbers: 250 puzzles. Success: MPNet embedding baseline 11.6%, GPT-3.5-Turbo 6.43%, GPT-4-Turbo 29.2%, GPT-4-Turbo with CoT 38.93% (p < 6.77e-5). Challenge variant: GPT-4-Turbo 25.56%, with CoT 23.46%. A word-order effect: sorting the words gave an identical 65% replication of a prior claim, unsorted only 3.33%.
limits: Success counts full solves under a mistake limit. Order effect shows the prior high number was an artefact. 2023-24 models.
agent_relevance: Guessing order and surface grouping can inflate scores. Hard variants remove the CoT benefit, so CoT is not a reframing tool.

source: Naeini et al. (2023) Large Language Models are Fixated by Red Herrings: Only Connect Wall dataset
finding: Removing the misleading items from the puzzle raises scores a lot, which is the machine version of a fixation (Einstellung) account. More in-context examples did not help.
numbers: 494 test walls (1,976 groups). Humans solved 285 walls, 1,405 groups (about 71%). GPT-4 best 272 groups (13.8%), 7 walls (5-shot). GPT-3.5 best 149 groups. Red herrings removed: GPT-4 0-shot on WordNet version 471 walls, 1,926 groups; on a randomised version 68 walls, 655 groups.
limits: Read through a fetched HTML extraction of the paper (ar5iv), not the PDF. No chain-of-thought tested. UK-centric. Authors do not directly test the Einstellung effect.
agent_relevance: Strong support that misleading surface cues drive failure, so cue-stripping (O6 restating without the lure) is a sensible operator to test.

source: Goldstein et al. (2023) Decoding Stumpers: Large Language Models vs. Human Problem-Solvers
finding: Chat models beat people at generating answers to one-step intuition riddles but are worse than people at telling right from wrong answers.
numbers: 81 human participants. Humans solved 38.15% (replicates the 35% of Bar-Hillel 2021). Models solved 26-58%; chat models (GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4) mean 57.8% on original set vs 29.6% for Davinci-2/3. Verification between two options: humans 100% when they had solved it, 63.8% when they had failed; most models below chance (mean 41%). Example pairs in the prompt helped GPT-3 models and hurt chat models (interaction F(1,4)=30.82, p=0.005).
limits: Few items; small per-cell n. 2023 models. 'Stumpers' are single-step riddles, close to insight but not the lab paradigms.
agent_relevance: Generation outruns verification, matching c02. Do not use the model as the verifier of its own insight.

source: Speed (2023) Assessing the nature of large language models: a caution against anthropocentrism
finding: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 were poor at the Remote Associates Test, better on five insight-style arithmetic/word problems, and unstable from one session to the next. GPT-3.5's insight scores moved opposite to human difficulty.
numbers: RAT: GPT-3.5 9-45% across four administrations; GPT-4 50% and 59%. Human per-triplet success 9-85%; correlation with GPT-3.5 r=0.39. Insight problems (5): GPT-3.5 1.5-3.5 correct across four runs, GPT-4 4.5/5 in one run; human per-problem 44-61%; correlation GPT-3.5 vs humans r=-0.63 (4 observations). Analytic problems: 0 correct.
limits: Preprint, tiny item sets, very few runs, answers often right with wrong explanation (not credited in RAT). Authors say the negative correlation should carry little weight.
agent_relevance: Run-to-run variance is large on these items, so any scaffold test needs many seeds.

source: Orru et al. (2023) Human-like problem-solving abilities in large language models using ChatGPT
finding: ChatGPT solved about as many verbal insight riddles as the typical human sample did. The authors read this as human-like.
numbers: 30 riddles from Ansburg and Dominowski (2000), 15 practice and 15 transfer. ChatGPT (Jan 9, 2023 version) 7/15 and 5/15. Human solution rate median 0.55 (IQR 0.23-0.64) and 0.35 (0.30-0.40), N=20 human rates from the original study. Practice-vs-transfer difference not significant for either.
limits: Read via a page extraction. Single model version, small human sample, riddles from 2000 so contamination is not ruled out. Statistics in the paper are inconsistent (p reported as 'p<0.72', two sets of z values). Some answers scored right despite contradictory reasoning. Conclusions go beyond 30 items.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence. Treat 'human-like on riddles' claims from 2023 as unproven for our agent; use our own held-out set.

source: Lee et al. (2025) Puzzled by Puzzles: When Vision-Language Models Can't Take a Hint (rebus puzzles)
finding: Rebus puzzles (a picture plus wordplay that must be re-read as a phrase) are hard even for the best reasoning models. Hints about the needed skill and one worked example barely help. Retrying with feedback gives small gains and then stalls.
numbers: 432 hand-made puzzles (333 original in the main set). Naive-match accuracy: GPT-5 60.42%, o3 54.56%, o4-mini 48.16%, Gemini-2.5-Pro 39.99%, GPT-4o 18.75%, Claude-3.7-Sonnet 10.20%. Humans: non-expert 16.4-37.23%, expert 76.4%. Skill-guided hint: GPT-4o 18.75 to 20.79, o4-mini 48.16 to 49.77, GPT-4o-mini 8.37 to 7.93. One in-context example: o4-mini 48.16 to 45.83. Captions instead of image: o4-mini 41.09.
quote: the primary bottleneck for VLMs ... may not be a failure to identify what kind of reasoning is needed
limits: Vision-language, so perception is mixed in. Human numbers are ranges from a different pool. Prompt variance acknowledged by the authors.
agent_relevance: Telling a model which re-representation is needed does not make it do it. Knowing vs executing is a gap, so operators need concrete outputs (a restated problem) that code can check.

source: Ji et al. (2025) MathSticks: A Benchmark for Visual Symbolic Compositional Reasoning with Matchstick Puzzles
finding: Matchstick equation repair (the Knoblich paradigm family) is hard for current vision-language models. Models stick to digit edits and rarely change the operator, which is the hardest constraint to relax in the human work.
numbers: 1.4M generated instances plus a curated test set; 14 models; 82.01% of instances need two-stick moves. With text prompt: o3 60.00%, Gemini-2.5-Pro 45.25%, Gemini-2.5-Flash 26.50%, o4-mini 24.75%, Seed-1.6-Thinking 21.50%, Seed-1.6 3.25%. Pure visual: o3 38.50%, Gemini-2.5-Pro 22.50%. Humans (3 adults) 91.72%. Errors seen: perception, illegal edits, arithmetic not re-checked (9-3=5 turned to 9-2=5), operator handling, bad output format.
quote: models are biased toward digit-level manipulations rather than considering operator edits
limits: Not Knoblich's exact problem types (no tightness manipulation reported). Only 3 human participants. Prose in the paper names Gemini for the one-move drop while the tables show the top row (o3) going 51.67 to 25.83.
agent_relevance: Direct machine analogue of constraint relaxation: the model does not drop the 'operators stay fixed' assumption. A slot that lists assumptions and forces an edit on each one is testable here (O4).

source: Ji et al. (2025) MathSticks, thinking vs base and multi-solution
finding: Reasoning variants of the same model beat base variants by a wide margin on this task. Instances with several valid answers are harder for models than unique-answer ones.
numbers: With text: Seed-1.6-Thinking 21.50% vs Seed-1.6 3.25%; Gemini-2.5-Pro 45.25% vs Gemini-2.5-Flash 26.50% (different sizes); o3 60.00% vs GPT-4o 0.00%. Multi-solution cases are 56.88% of the data.
limits: Pairs are not always matched models. Training data may include matchstick-like puzzles.
agent_relevance: Search over edits with a code checker (arithmetic is exactly checkable) fits this task and removes the arithmetic-verification error.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction in Large Language Models
finding: Asking the model first for the general principle behind the question, then answering with it, beats plain and chain-of-thought prompting on physics, chemistry and multi-hop QA. This is the most direct prompt-level re-representation method in LLM work.
numbers: PaLM-2L: MMLU Physics 66.4 to 73.2, Chemistry 70.9 to 81.8, TimeQA 41.5 to 66.0. GPT-4: Physics 69.4 base, 82.9 CoT, 84.5 step-back; Chemistry 80.9 base, 85.3 CoT, 85.6 step-back. Error analysis (MMLU Physics, PaLM-2L): fixes 20.5% of baseline errors, introduces 11.9%. One exemplar is enough.
limits: Gain over CoT for GPT-4 is only 1.6 and 0.3 points. Not tested on insight puzzles. Abstraction is not the same as constraint relaxation or chunk decomposition.
agent_relevance: Supports O2 (generalise) and O6 as a cheap first re-representation. It also shows the cost: about 12% new errors, so check outputs.

source: Abhinav P M et al. (2025) The Riddle of Reflection: Evaluating Reasoning and Self-Awareness in Multilingual LLMs using Indian Riddles
finding: Prompting style barely matters on riddles. The strongest model is the most overconfident when asked to check its own wrong answers.
numbers: 96 original riddles per language, 7 Indian languages, 5 models, 7 prompting strategies. Gemini 2.5 Pro initial accuracy 39.09%, true-negative rate 4.34% (it confirms its wrong answers over 95% of the time). Llama-4-Scout accuracy 9.95%, true-negative rate 42.09%. Gemini 2.5 Pro: zero-shot 41.52% vs 2-shot random 42.11%. Context-reconstructed examples gave no consistent advantage.
limits: Self-evaluation uses the model's own yes/no on its own answer. Multilingual, culturally specific riddles.
agent_relevance: Same direction as c14 and c02: self-checking of riddle answers is unreliable, and best models are worst at it.

source: Liu, Lee, et al. (2025) No Evidence for LLMs Being Useful in Problem Reframing (CHI 2025)
finding: In a human-designer study, three ways of using LLMs for problem reframing, including one built on a theory of reframing, did not improve the quality of problem frames. LLM use widened the gap between experienced and inexperienced designers.
numbers: N=280 designers; three LLM conditions (free-form, direct generation, theory-structured). Effect sizes not seen.
limits: Only the abstract was read (full PDF download failed). Human designers using LLMs, not an LLM solving by itself. Design problems, not insight puzzles.
agent_relevance: Matches the SCHEMA note that LLM reframing (O8) showed a null result in a large test. Keep O8 behind a gate.

source: Ollinger, Jones, Knoblich (2006) Heuristics and representational change in two-move matchstick arithmetic tasks (human background for the machine tests)
finding: Difficulty of two-move matchstick problems is set by how much representational change is needed, not by how good the heuristics are. The authors propose that representational change is a precondition for heuristics to be useful.
numbers: N=120 problem solvers, two types of two-move problems (from the abstract in search results).
limits: Abstract-level only. Not read in full this session.
agent_relevance: A worked order: first change the representation, then run heuristics. Suggests the agent should not apply search heuristics inside a frame that is already failing.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider, Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Four matchstick arithmetic experiments supported two mechanisms of representational change: relaxing constraints and decomposing tight perceptual chunks. Problem types differ in which constraint or chunk must be changed.
numbers: Not read here; the human numbers belong to angle A or B.
limits: Search result and abstract only in this angle.
agent_relevance: The paradigm that MathSticks (c18) and NazoNazo (c01) borrow. Their machine failures map to the same two mechanisms.

source: ContextMatters (2025) LLM proposes functionally equivalent goals that loosen constraints, checked by a classical planner (arXiv 2506.15828)
finding: An LLM proposes relaxed or equivalent goals when the original goal cannot be reached, and a classical planner checks feasibility. This is constraint relaxation used inside an agent loop with an outside checker.
numbers: Reported +52.45% success-rate improvement over an LLM-plus-PDDL baseline (search snippet only).
limits: Search snippet only; robotics with 3D scene graphs. Not an insight task.
agent_relevance: A working pattern for O4: the model drops a constraint, code verifies what the relaxed problem permits. Related LLM-Flax (2604.26569) and AutoCO (2509.12643) use the same split.

source: Cross-study synthesis, angle C: where machines fail on representation-change tasks
finding: Across c01, c07, c08, c13, c17, c18 the same pattern appears. Models fail when a surface cue or default assumption must be dropped. They improve when the lure is removed or the item is familiar.
numbers: Humans vs best model on comparable sets: NazoNazo 52.9% vs 17.6% mean reasoning models; Only Connect 71% vs 13.8% of groups; MathSticks 91.72% vs 60% (best model, with text); BrainTeaser 92% vs about 53-63%.
limits: Different tasks, different scoring, different dates. No common scale.
agent_relevance: Our own re-representation test set should include a lure-removed twin of each item, so we can tell fixation from plain difficulty.

source: Cross-study synthesis, angle C: what prompts moved results
finding: Prompts that restate the problem at a different level (step-back, c20), give structure-matched examples (c09) or give a worked questioning transcript (c11) gave gains of roughly 2 to 15 points. Skill hints, plain few-shot and generic reflection gave about 0 to 3 points (c17, c06, c21, c07).
numbers: Step-back +7 to +11 points PaLM-2L MMLU, +25 TimeQA; RISCORE +2 to +10; SPLAT word puzzles +5 to +12; skill hint +1.6 to +2.0 (rebus); forced reconsideration math +8.4, crosswords +0.45.
limits: Mixed models and benchmarks; many gains are small and un-replicated; baselines differ.
agent_relevance: Rank the operators to test: restate/abstract first, matched example retrieval second, generic 'reconsider' last.

source: Cross-study synthesis, angle C: gaps found
finding: Searches found no study that runs Knoblich's actual matchstick types (A to D, tight chunks) on language models, no LLM test of the Luchins or classic eye-movement style fixation, and no LLM-agent paper that implements chunk decomposition by name. The closest are MathSticks (c18), Only Connect (c13) and cryptic crosswords (c04).
numbers: Not applicable.
limits: Search tools returned snippets only for several queries; absence is not proof.
agent_relevance: An open experiment for us: run Knoblich-type matchstick items with and without an operator-edit slot, scored by exact arithmetic check.
